name: Eyepatchmaxxing

lead: Eyepatchmaxxing is the practice of wearing an eyepatch as a fashion or image choice. In looksmaxxing forums, the stated appeal is concealment: a patch covers one eye, so asymmetry or an eye area someone dislikes is hidden, and the patch becomes the focal point instead.

The idea draws on the long cultural image of the patch as a mark of mystery, from fiction to well-known wearers. Discussion is limited to a few forum threads; no studies have looked at how eyepatches affect perceived attractiveness.

paras: Wearers choose a patch (cloth, leather or adhesive) and wear it as part of an outfit. Forum users describe it as an option for people with eye asymmetry who want to cover the less-liked eye.

Covering one eye removes binocular vision, which reduces depth perception and the visible field on that side. Adhesive patches can irritate skin. Forum replies show the idea is contested, with some users treating it as a joke and others as a camouflage option.

chain: Asymmetry or disliked eye is hidden
Patch becomes the focal point of the face
angle.text: Proponents say a patch hides an asymmetrical or less-liked eye and substitutes a deliberate style statement. This is a claim from forum discussion; its effect on perceived attractiveness has not been measured.

lead: Eyepatchmaxxing is a style practice in which a person wears an eyepatch to change how their face reads. On looksmax.org it is discussed as a way to hide eye asymmetry: one user replied that a patch could help cover up asymmetrical eyes, and the thread's original poster said that was the reason they were trying them.[1]

An eyepatch is a small patch worn over one eye, held by a band, string or adhesive. Historically it was used by people who had lost an eye, and today it is also used medically, for example to treat amblyopia in children or to ease double vision.[2] In fiction it is commonly used to add mystery to a character.[2]

paras: The eyepatch has a long history as a practical item. Before modern surgery, patches were common among soldiers and sailors who had lost an eye, and the popular pirate image owes much to nineteenth-century novels.[2] Pilots have also covered one eye to keep it dark-adapted.[2]

The only community material on the practice is a looksmax.org thread asking whether eyepatchmaxxing is legitimate. One reply suggested it could help cover asymmetry, the poster said that was their intent, and another replied sarcastically about everyone wearing patches on a Friday night, showing that the idea is met with humour as well as interest.[1]
No studies found. Clinical research on eyepatches concerns medical patching for amblyopia and double vision, not appearance.[2]

Medical sources note that covering one eye is a treatment tool that changes how the eyes work together, as in amblyopia therapy.[2] Wearing a patch day to day removes binocular input on the covered side.

lore.intro: Discussion is confined to a small number of forum posts.[1]

claims.claim: A patch can cover asymmetrical eyes
